h1: Changing career to brewing in your 30s or 40s
title: Changing Career to Brewing at 30 or 40 | Craft Beer School
desc: Moving into brewing in your 30s or 40s: what you bring, what to expect, how to test the idea cheaply and how to plan the money.
teaser: You are not too late. Mid-career changers bring skills breweries need. A plan makes the move less risky.
standfirst: Moving into brewing later in life is common. This guide helps you decide how, in what role and with what safety net.
sections:
Brewing needs people who can run a process, count accurately and talk to customers. If you have worked in finance, engineering, retail, hospitality, logistics or health care, you carry skills that breweries need. Process discipline helps in the brewhouse. Sales experience helps in the taproom and with distributors. A technical background helps in quality.

Name your three most transferable skills and write them in the first lines of your CV.

One more asset is professionalism. You know how to handle a difficult customer, finish a report and own a mistake. Brewery owners value staff who do those plain things well.

Brewing is physical. A day often means lifting sacks of malt, hauling hoses, cleaning tanks and standing on a wet floor for hours. The glamorous part is a small share of the week. If you have a bad back or a long commute, plan for it.

Many brewers start in packaging or cellar work. It takes time to move into the brewhouse. Expect to be the newest person in the room even if you managed a team in your last job.

Hours can be unsocial, since brew days start early and taprooms run through evenings and weekends. Talk to your family about it before you apply, not after your first double shift.

Before you resign, spend a few weekends in a brewery. Offer to volunteer on a brew day or work a taproom shift. Brew at home if your country allows it. Take a short course to learn the language. A few months of this tells you whether you enjoy the work, not just the idea of it.

Read learning to brew while working full time for how to do this around a job.
Choose a role, not just an industry

Brewing is a business with many roles: brewer, cellar hand, packaging operator, quality technician, sales representative, taproom manager, supply planner. You may suit one of those more than the brewhouse. Look at working in beer sales and working in brewery supply chain and planning before you set your heart on mashing in.

A career change is easier when your old skill gives you a head start in the new role.

Entry-level brewery pay is often below what an experienced professional earns elsewhere. We do not quote figures, since they vary by country and company. Work out the minimum income your household needs and how many months you can stay below your old salary.

Keep a financial cushion. Consider part-time work in the industry while you keep a main income. Check any visa or work permit rules if you plan to move countries.

Ask yourself what would make you stop. A fixed review date, such as a year from now, turns a vague worry into a plan.
Training that fits an adult life

Structured learning shortens the path. Choose a programme with live classes, recordings you can replay and assignments that give you something to show an employer. Weekend classes suit people with jobs. Avoid anything that promises a job on completion, because no course can promise that honestly.

Brewing Fundamentals runs as a four-week live online course. Students join from their own time zone. Recordings cover missed classes.

Ask questions of any programme: who teaches, how many students are in a class, what you will have produced at the end and how missed sessions are handled. A small class lets you ask about your own situation.

• Complete a structured course while you work.
  • Volunteer weekly at a brewery.
  • Brew on a small system if the law allows.
  • Tell people in your network that you are looking.
  • Apply for roles that value your old skills as well as your new ones.

If you are ready to make the move, a structured start saves months of trial and error. Reserve your seat in the next batch and use the weeks before it begins to volunteer.

Review at six months. If the work still pulls you, plan the next step. If it does not, you have spent little and learned a lot, which is an acceptable result.
faqs: Am I too old to become a brewer?
No. Many people join in their 30s, 40s and beyond. Be ready for physical work and a junior start.
Should I quit my job first?
Test the idea part-time before you decide. Keep a financial cushion either way.
Many do, especially people with skills in operations, sales, quality or finance.
Is a course enough to get hired?
A course is a strong start, but practical hours in a brewery matter too.
